label: th:l1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:l1}The bounded set $A\subset \ell^1$ is relatively compact if and only if 
\[
\forall_{\varepsilon>0} \exists_{N\in\mathbb{N}} \forall_{x\in A} \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty} |x_n|<\varepsilon. 
\]
head: environment

label: th:c0
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:c0}The bounded set $A\subset c_0$ is relatively compact if and only if 
\[
\forall_{\varepsilon>0} \exists_{N\in\mathbb{N}} \forall_{x\in A} |x_n|<\varepsilon. 
\]
head: environment

label: th:old:linf
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:old:linf}The bounded set $A\subset \ell^\infty$ is relatively compact if and only if for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists finite family of sets $U_i\subset\mathbb{N}$, $i=1,...,N$, such that $\mathbb{N} = \bigcup_{i=1}^N U_i$ and
\[
\forall_{x,y\in A} \forall_{i=1,...,N} \sup_{n\in U_i}|x_n-y_n|<\varepsilon. 
\]

title: Definition
body_md: The family $\mathcal{F}$ is called {\em hereditary} if for any $F\in\mathcal{F}$ and $G\subset F$ there is $G\in\mathcal{F}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: We call the family $\mathcal{F}$ {\em compact} if the set of characteristic functions $\{\mathbbm{1}_F : F\in\mathcal{F}\}\subset C(\mathbb{N})$ is compact in the pointwise convergence topology.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: The family $\mathcal{F}$ is compact if and only if the closure of the set $\{\mathbbm{1}_F : F\in\mathcal{F}\}$ in $C(\mathbb{N})$ with pointise convergence topology consists of characteristic functions of finite sets only.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\phi$ be a non-pathological lsc submeasure. Define a function $\hat\phi:\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}\to[0,\infty]$ by:
\[
\hat\phi(x)=\sup\left\{\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\mu(\{n\})|x_n|: \mu\in\mathcal{M}_\phi\right\}
\]
for all $x=(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$. Define also:
\[
\mathrm{FIN}(\phi)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}: \hat\phi(x)<\infty\right\};
\]
\[
\mathrm{EXH}(\phi)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}: \lim_{n\to\infty}\hat\phi(x\cdot\chi_{[n+1, +\infty)})=0\right\} =\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}: \lim_{n\to\infty}\hat\phi(P_n(x))=0\right\}.
\]
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Letting $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of finite sets covering $\mathbb{N}$, it is possible to define a norm on $\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$ as follows: $$\Vert x\Vert_\mathcal{F}=\sup_{F \in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{n \in F} |x_n|.$$ Then the space $$X_\mathcal{F}=\{x \in \mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}: \, \lim_{n \to \infty} \Vert x \cdot \mathbbm{1}_{[n+1, +\infty)}\Vert_\mathcal{F}=0\}.$$ is called a \emph{combinatorial Banach space}.
head: environment

label: th:cominatorial:submeasure
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:cominatorial:submeasure}
    Combinatorial Banach spaces are a subclass of submeasure sequence spaces.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us define a submeasure $\Phi_\mathcal{F}$ as $\Phi_\mathcal{F}(C)=\sup_{F \in \mathcal{F}}|C\cap F|$. It is trivial to check that this is indeed a submeasure and that it is lsc.
Moreover, for any $F\in\mathcal{F}$ we have a measure $\mu_F$ defined on $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$
by $\mu_F(C) = |C\cap F|$. It is easy to observe that $\mu_F(C)\leq\Phi_\mathcal{F}(C)$ for all $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ and $F\in\mathcal{F}$ and that
\[
\Phi_{\mathcal{F}}(C) = \sup_{F\in\mathcal{F}}\mu_F(C).
\]
This shows that $\Phi_\mathcal{F}$ is nonpathological. Moreover, it is obvoius that for any sequence $x\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ there is $\hat\Phi_\mathcal{F}(x) = \Vert x\Vert_\mathcal{F}$. That's why  $X_\mathcal{F}=\mathrm{EXH}(\Phi_\mathcal{F})$
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Since now we will denote the combinatorial Banach space $X_\mathcal{F}$ by $\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ (instead of $\mathrm{EXH}(\Phi_\mathcal{F})$. Consequently we will write $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ instead of $\mathrm{FIN}(\Phi_\mathcal{F})$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The topological spaces  $K_\mathcal{F}$ and $K_\mathcal{G}$ constructed for different families $\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}$ of finite sets covering $\mathbb{N}$ are formally different, even when $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ have the same hereditary closure.
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md: Assume $\mathcal{F}$ is hereditary. Then the set $K$ is compact if and only if the family $\mathcal{F}$ is compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of compactness of $K$ for compact $\mathcal{F}$ is given in the mentioned paper \cite{KKLPB} but we will state it here for completeness (in much simpler version adjusted to the present context). And we will start with a proof in this direction: assume that $\mathcal{F}$ is compact and take a sequence $(\xi_n)\subset K$ convergent to some $\eta\in\tilde K$. We are going to show that $\eta\in K$. Let us fix any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and take $\delta < 4^{-k}$. We know that for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ big enough we have for all $j\in[1,k]$
\[
|\eta_j-\xi_{n,j}|<\delta
\]
what, taking into account that either  $\xi_{n,j}=0$ (when $j\not\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)$) or $|\xi_n,j|>\delta$ (when $j\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)$), means that $\eta_j=0$ iff $\xi_{n,j}=0$ for $n$ big enough and for all $j\in\mathbb{N}$. Hence ${\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)\cap [1,k] ={\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)\cap[1,k]$. But we know that ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)\in\mathcal{F}$ so, because $\mathcal{F}$ is hereditary, also ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)\cap[1,k]\in\mathcal{F}$. This means that for each $k\in\mathbb{N}$ the set ${\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)\cap[1,k]\in\mathcal{F}$. It is easy to observe that the characteristic function $\mathbbm{1}_{{\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)}$ is a pointwise limit of the sequence of characteristic functions $\mathbbm{1}_{{\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)\cap[1,n]}$, meaning that ${\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)$ belongs to the closure of the family $\mathcal{F}$. Since $\mathcal{F}$ is compact the set ${\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)$ must be finite. This means that 
$\eta\in K$, and thus $K$ is closed and compact as a subset of a compact space $\tilde K$.

Now let us assume $\mathcal{F}$ is not compact, so there exists such $G\subset\mathbb{N}$ that $|G|=\infty$ and $\mathbbm{1}_G(k) = \lim_{n\to+\infty}\mathbbm{1}_{F_n}(k)$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and for a certain sequence $(F_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\subset\mathcal{F}$. Then the sequences $\mathbbm{1}_{F_n}\in K$, the sequence $\mathbbm{1}_G$ is a pointwise limit of $(\mathbbm{1}_{F_n})$ in $\tilde K$ and  $\mathbbm{1}_G\not\in K$. Hence, $K$ is not compact.
head: environment

label: exh:fun:representation
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will prove this Lemma in a series of steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\item 
Let us first define the map $\Phi\colon c_{00}\to BC(K)$ by
\[
\Phi(a)(\xi) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}} a_n\xi_n
\]
for $a\in c_{00}$ and $\xi\in K$.  Since ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)$ is finite for any $\xi\in K$, the sum is well defined for any sequence $a\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}$. We need to prove that $\Phi$ indeed falls into $BC(K)$.

First, we will show that for any $a\in c_{00}$ the function $\Phi(a):K\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous. Let us take any sequence $\xi_n\to\xi$ in $K$. Since $\xi\in K$, we know that  ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\subset [1,k]$ for some $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\in\mathcal{F}$. We also know that ${\operatorname{supp}}(a)\subset[1,j]$ for some $j\in\mathbb{N}$. We can also observe that for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ big enough the sequence $\xi_n$ is constant on the interval $[1,\max\{j,k\}]$ meaning that
\[
\lim_{n\to+\infty} \Phi(a)(\xi_n) = \lim_{n\to+\infty} \sum_{i=1}^{\max\{j,k\}} a_i\xi_{n,i} = \sum_{i=1}^{\max\{j,k\}} a_i\xi_{i} = \Phi(a)(\xi).
\]

We should also observe that $\Phi(a)\colon K\to\mathbb{R}$ is a bounded function. Let us take any $a\in c_{00}$ and any $\xi\in K$. Then 
\[
|\Phi(a)(\xi)| = \left| \sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}} a_i\xi_i \right| \leq \sum_{i\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} |a_i|\cdot|\xi_i|  \leq \norm{a}_\mathcal{F},
\]
because ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\in\mathcal{F}$ and $\norm{\xi}_\infty\leq 1$.
As we can see, this estimate works also for any $a\in \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ (so also for any $a\in\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$).

This means we have a map $\Phi:c_{00}\to BC(K)$.
\item The map $\Phi:c_{00}\to BC(K)$ is obviously linear, now we are going to show that it is continuous when $c_{00}$ is endowed with a norm $\norm{\cdot}_\mathcal{F}$. Let us take such $a\in c_{00}$ that $\norm{a}_\mathcal{F}\leq 1$. Then 
\[
\norm{\Phi(a)}_{\infty} = \sup_{\xi\in K} |\Phi(a)(\xi)|.
\]

Let us fix $\xi\in K$ and estimate
\[
|\Phi(a)(\xi)| = \left| \sum_{i\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} a_i\xi_i \right| \leq
\left(\sup_{i\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)}|\xi_i|\right) \cdot \left( \sum_{i\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} |a_i| \right) \leq \Vert a\Vert_\mathcal{F}
\]
since $|\xi_i|\leq 1$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$ and ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\in\mathcal{F}$. This means that $\Phi:c_{00}\to BC(K)$ is linear and continuous with a norm $\Vert \Phi\Vert\leq 1$.

\item We can see that $c_{00}$ is dense in $\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ so for each $a\in\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ there exists a sequence $a_n \in c_{00}$ such that $\norm{a_n-a}_\mathcal{F}\to 0$. Moreover, for any fixed $\xi\in K$ we have ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\in\mathcal{F}$ being a finite set, what means that
\[
\Phi(a)(\xi) = \lim_{n\to +\infty} \Phi(a_n)(\xi)
\]
is well defined. Moreover we may take $a_n$ in such a way that $\norm{a_n}_\mathcal{F} \leq \norm{a}_\mathcal{F}$ (e.g. by taking $a_n=a\cdot \mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}$). Then we can see that for $n$ big enough we have ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\subset[1,n]$, $a_k=a_{n,k}$ for $k\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)$ and consequently 
\[
\left|\Phi(a)(\xi)\right| = \left| \sum_{i\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} a_i\xi_i \right| =  \left| \sum_{i\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} a_{n,i}\xi_i \right| \leq \norm{a_n}_\mathcal{F} \leq \norm{a}_\mathcal{F}.
\]
Hence $\Vert \Phi(a)\Vert_{\infty} \leq \norm{a}_\mathcal{F}$ for any $a\in\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$.

\item Let us now prove that $\Vert \Phi(a)\Vert_{\infty} \geq \norm{a}_\mathcal{F}$ for any $a\in\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$. Let us take any $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $F\in\mathcal{F}$ that $\sum_{j\in F}|a_j|\geq (1-\varepsilon)\norm{a}_\mathcal{F}$. Then 
we may take such $\eta\in K$ that
\[
\eta_n = \begin{cases} 1 & n\in F \wedge a_n>0\cr
-1 & n\in F \wedge a_n<0\cr
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
Then we have $\eta\in K$ and
\[
\Vert\Phi(a)\Vert_\infty \geq \left|\sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}} a_n\eta_n\right| = \sum_{n\in F}|a_n|\geq (1-\varepsilon)\norm{a}_\mathcal{F}.
\]
Since the inequality given above is correct for any $\varepsilon(0,1)$ we can see that $\Vert \Phi(a)\Vert_{\infty} \geq \norm{a}_\mathcal{F}$.



\item Since $\Phi$ is an isometry it is invertible on its range  and this observation completes the proof.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The main obstacle when trying to repeat this construction for the space $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ is that if $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})\neq \mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$, then the space $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ is not separable (see Theorem 5.4 in \cite{FBN}).
head: environment

label: rem:not:continuous
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:not:continuous}
    The proof of Lemma \ref{exh:fun:representation} may not be easily repeated for the space $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$. Moreover, it appears that the map $\Phi$ is not necessarily defined to the space $BC(K)$. We can easily see that for any $a\in\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ the function $\Phi(a)\colon K\to\mathbb{R}$ is well defined and bounded, but it appears it is not necessarily continuous. Let us take a  family $\mathcal{F}$ containing sets in the form $F_n=\{1,n\}$ for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and such that the cardinality of sets belonging to $\mathcal{F}$ is bounded by some constant. Then the constant sequence $a_n=1$ belongs to $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$, but the function $\Phi(a)$ is not continuous. To see this, let us take the sequence $(\xi_n)\subset K$, $\xi_{n,k}=\mathbbm{1}_{F_n}(k)$. As we can see $\xi_n\to\xi$, where $\xi_k = \mathbbm{1}_{\{1\}}(k)$. But $\Phi(a)(\xi_n)=2\not\to \Phi(a)(\xi)=1$.

title: Remark
body_md: The condition $(\ref{compact:bc}.1)$ in Theorem \ref{compact:bc} is satisfied  if and only if $A\subset \mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ is bounded.
head: environment

label: rem:uniform:limit
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:uniform:limit}The condition $(\ref{compact:bc}.2)$ in Theorem \ref{compact:bc} states that all of the sets $K_i$ are open in a product topology. This means that there exists such $n_0\in\mathbb{N}$ that for all $n\geq n_0$ and for $i\in\{1,...,N\}$ all the projections of $K_i$ into $n$-th coordinate equals to $D_n$. 
Hence, assume now that for a fixed $\varepsilon>0$ condition (\ref{compact:bc}.2) is satisfied.
This in turn implies that for a fixed $\varepsilon>0$ there exists such $n_0\in\mathbb{N}$ that for any fixed $i\in\{1,...,N\}$, any $a\in A$ and any $F\in\mathcal{F}$ such that $F\cap[n_0+1,\infty)\neq\emptyset$ we may take $\xi,\eta\in K$ such that ${\operatorname{supp}}\xi = {\operatorname{supp}}\eta = F$, $\xi_n=\eta_n=1$ for $n\in F\cap\{1,...,n_0\}$ and
\[
\xi_n = \begin{cases}
    1 & a_n \geq 0 \cr -1 & a_n < 0,
\end{cases}
\]
and $\eta_n=-\xi_n$. We can see that since $\xi$ and $\eta$ are identical on first $n_0$ coordinates, then they belong to the same set $K_i$. Then we have 
\[
\varepsilon > |\Phi(a)(\xi)-\Phi(a)(\eta)| = \left| \sum_{n\in F} a_n(\xi_n-\eta_n) \right| = 
2\sum_{n\in F\cap[n_0+1,+\infty)} |a_n|.
\]
Hence we may observe that if the condition $(\ref{compact:bc}.2)$ is satisfied then the limit 
\[
\lim_{n \to \infty} \Vert a \cdot \mathbbm{1}_{[n+1,+\infty)\}}\Vert_{\mathcal{F}} = 0
\]
is uniform with respect to elements $a\in A$.

label: th:compact:exh
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Obviously the statement that $A\subset \mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ is relatively compact is equivalent to saying that $\Phi(A)\subset BC(K)$ is relatively compact. Since for bounded $A$ the set $\Phi(A)(K)\subset\mathbb{R}$ is automatically bounded it is enough to focus on proving the conditions $(\ref{compact:bc}.2)$ and (\ref{th:compact:exh}.2) are equivalent.   

 If $\Phi(A)\subset BC(K)$ is relatively compact, then by Theorem \ref{compact:bc} the condition (\ref{compact:bc}.2) is satisfied, and repeating the reasoning given in  Remark \ref{rem:uniform:limit} we can see that condition $(\ref{th:compact:exh}.2)$ is satisfied as well.

 On the other hand, let us assume that condition $(\ref{th:compact:exh}.2)$ is satisfied for $\varepsilon/2$. Let us denote the projection from $K$ to the product $\prod_{i=1}^n D_i$ by $\Pi_n\colon K\to \prod_{i=1}^n D_i$ and let us take the set $\Xi\subset \prod_{i=1}^n D_i$ given by $\Xi = \Pi_n(K)$. The set $\Xi$ is finite and we may use its elements to build the open cover $K_{\hat\xi}$ of $K$ and indexed by elements $\hat\xi\in\Xi$. Let us take
 \[
 K_{\hat\xi} = \{ \xi\in K : \xi_k = \hat\xi(k) {\text{\ for\ }} k\in[1,n] \} = \{\hat\xi\}\times\Pi_{i=n+1}^\infty D_i.
 \]
 There are finitely many such sets, all of them are open and their sum covers entire space $K$. Now let us take any two sequences $\xi,\eta\in K_{\hat\xi}$ and any $a\in A$. Then we have
 \[
 |\Phi(a)(\xi)-\Phi(a)(\eta)| = \left| \sum_{k=1}^n (\xi_k-\eta_k)a_k + \sum_{k=n+1}^{+\infty} (\xi_k-\eta_k)a_k \right| \leq 
 \]
 \[
 \sum_{k=n+1}^{+\infty} |\xi_k| |a_k| + \sum_{k=n+1}^{+\infty} |\eta_k| |a_k| \leq
 \sum_{k\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)\cap[n+1,\infty)} |a_k| + \sum_{k\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\eta)\cap[n+1,\infty)} |a_k| \leq 2\cdot \frac{\varepsilon}{2},
 \]
 what completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:exh:compact:cond
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us first prove the implication $(ii)\Rightarrow (i)$. Let us first take any $\varepsilon>0$ and assume the condition $(ii)$ is satisfied for $\varepsilon/3$ and fix $n\in\mathbb{N}$.  Let us define the seminorm induced by a set of all nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ being the intersections $F\cap[1,n]$, where $F\in\mathcal{F}$ i.e. 
\[
\mathcal{B} = \{ F\cap [1,n] : F\in\mathcal{F} \wedge F\cap[1,n]\neq\emptyset \}.
\]
Let us take any $a,b\in A$. There exists such $F\in\mathcal{F}$ that 
\[
\sum_{k\in F} |a_k-b_k|\geq \Vert a-b\Vert_\mathcal{F} -\frac{\varepsilon}{3}.
\]
On the other hand we have
\[
\Vert a-b\Vert_{\mathcal{B}} \geq \sum_{k\in F\cap[1,n]}|a_k-b_k| =   
\sum_{k\in F}|a_k-b_k| - \sum_{k\in F\cap[n+1,\infty)}|a_k-b_k| \geq 
\]
\[
\sum_{k\in F}|a_k-b_k|  - \sum_{k\in F\cap[n+1,\infty)}|a_k|  - \sum_{k\in F\cap[n+1,\infty)}|b_k| \geq \Vert a-b\Vert_\mathcal{F} -\frac{\varepsilon}{3} -\frac{\varepsilon}{3}-\frac{\varepsilon}{3},
\]
hence $A-A$ is equinormed.

Let us now proceed to the proof of the implication $(i)\Rightarrow (ii)$. We will show that if we assume, contrary to our claim, that $(ii)$ is not satisfied, then the set $A$ may not be relatively compact. This, in turn, will contradict that $A-A$ is equinormed. So, if $(ii)$ is not satisfied then, for certain $\delta>0$ and  for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there exist $F_n\in\mathcal{F}$ and $a_n\in A$ such that 
\[
\sum_{k\in[n+1,\infty)\cap F_n} |a_{n,k}|>\delta.
\]
We will show that the sequence $(a_n)\subset A$ may not contain a convergent subsequence. We will show that for any $n\in\mathbb{N}$ there exists $m_n>n$ such that for all $k\geq m_n$
\[
\Vert a_n-a_k\Vert_\mathcal{F} \geq \frac{\delta}{2} > 0.
\]
For any fixed $n\in\mathbb{N}$, since $a_n\in\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ there exists  $m_n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that 
\[
\Vert a_n\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[m_n,\infty)}\Vert_{\mathcal{F}} <\frac{\delta}{2}
\]
We may of course assume that $m_n>n$. Then for any $k\geq m_n$ we have 
\[
\Vert a_n-a_k\Vert_\mathcal{F} \geq \sum_{i\in [k,\infty)\cap F_k}|a_{n,i}-a_{k,i}|\geq
\sum_{i\in [k,\infty)\cap F_k}|a_{k,i}|- \sum_{i\in [k,\infty)\cap F_k}|a_{n,i}|
\geq \delta - \frac{\delta}{2}.
\]
This shows that $(a_n)$ does not contain any Cauchy subsequence.

title: Theorem

label: fin:fun:representation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{fin:fun:representation}
The space $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ is isomorphic to the appropriate subspace of the space $B(K)$ of bounded functions $f\colon K\to\mathbb{R}$ endowed with a supremum norm.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We will do it in a series of steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\item 
Let us first define the map $\Phi\colon \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})\to B(K)$ by
\[
\Phi(a)(\xi) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{N}} a_n\xi_n = \sum_{n\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} a_n\xi_n
\]
for $a\in\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ and $\xi\in K$. Since ${\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)$ is finite for any $\xi\in K$ the sum is well defined for any sequence $a\in\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$. 

We can see that for any $a\in\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ and $\xi\in K$
\[
|\Phi(a)(\xi)| = \left| \sum_{n\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} a_n\xi_n \right| \leq  \sum_{n\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi)} |a_n| \leq\Vert a\Vert_{\mathcal{F}},
\]
what means that $\Phi(a)\in B(K)$.


\item The map $\Phi:\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})\to B(K)$ is obviously linear, now we are going to show that it is continuous. Let us take any $a\in \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$. Then 
\[
\norm{\Phi(a)}_{\infty} = \sup_{\xi\in K} |\Phi(a)(\xi)| \leq \Vert a\Vert_\mathcal{F}.
\]
This means $\Phi$ is linear and continuous with a norm $\Vert \Phi\Vert\leq 1$.


\item Similarly as in the proof of Lemma \ref{exh:fun:representation} we can see that $\Phi$ is an isometry and it is invertible (from its image). The proof is identical, so it will not be repeated.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: fin:cont:function:space
title: Lemma
body_md: \label{fin:cont:function:space}Assume $K$ is endowed with $d_\infty$ metric. Then, for $a\in\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ the map $\Phi(a):K\to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\xi_n\to\xi_0$ in $K$, i.e. $d_\infty(\xi_n,\xi_0)\to 0$. Let us take any $\varepsilon>0$. Then for $n\in\mathbb{N}$ big enough we know that $\xi_{n,k}$ is constant, i.e. $\xi_{n,k}=\xi_{0,k}$ for $k\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_0)$ and   $|\xi_{n,k}|<\frac{\epsilon}{\Vert a\Vert_\mathcal{F}}$   for $k\not\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_0)$. Then
\[
|\Phi(a)(\xi_n)-\Phi(a)(\xi_0)|\leq \sum_{k\not\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_0)}|a_k| |\xi_{n,k}|
=\sum_{k\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)\setminus {\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_0)} |a_k| |\xi_{n,k}| 
\]
\[
\leq \frac{\epsilon}{\Vert a\Vert_\mathcal{F}} \sum_{k\in{\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_n)\setminus {\operatorname{supp}}(\xi_0)} |a_k| \leq \varepsilon.
\]
This actually shows that $\Phi(a)$ is a continuous function.

head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: By Lemma \ref{fin:cont:function:space} the compactness criteria given in Theorem \ref{th:compact:b}  may be enhanced a little: we may require that the finite cover $\{K_1,\ldots,K_N\}$ be composed of subsets $K_i\subset K$ open in the metric space $(K,d_\infty)$.
head: environment

label: prop:fin:exh:equinormed
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:fin:exh:equinormed}
If $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})\neq\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$, then there exists such $A\subset\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ that $A$ is equinormed and $A$ is not relatively compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $x\in\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})\setminus\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$. This means that there exist $c>0$ and a sequence $F_n\in\mathcal{F}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{k\in F_n \cap [n+1,+\infty)} |a_k| \geq c.
\]     
Let $A=\{ x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]} : n\in \mathbb{N}\}.$ As we can see, $A$ is equinormed, since there exists such $F_0\in\mathcal{F}$ that
\[
\sum_{k\in F_0} |x_k| \geq \Vert x\Vert_\mathcal{F}-\varepsilon 
\]
for $\varepsilon\in(0,c)$.
When $n\geq \max F_0$, then
\[
\sum_{k\in F_0} |x_k\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}(k)| = \sum_{k\in F_0} |x_k| \geq \Vert x\Vert_\mathcal{F}-\varepsilon \geq  \Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}\Vert_\mathcal{F}-\varepsilon. 
\]
On the other hand, let us take
 such a finite family $\mathcal{B} \subset \mathcal{F}$ that each set $B_0 \in \{ F\cap [1,\max F_0] : F\in\mathcal{F} \}$ is represented by some $B\in\mathcal{B}$ such that $B_0 = B\cap [1,\max F_0]$. More formally:
 $$(\tau \subseteq [1,\max F_0] \land \, \exists T \in \mathcal{F}: \; \tau \subseteq T) \implies \exists B \in \mathcal{B}: \; \tau \subseteq B.$$ Then $\mathcal{B}$ is a finite family and we have 
\[
\Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}\Vert_{\mathcal{B}} = \Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}\Vert_{\mathcal{F}}  \geq \Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}\Vert_{\mathcal{F}} - \varepsilon 
\]
for all $n\leq \max F_0$. This proves that $A$ is equinormed. But $A-A$ is not equinormed, since for any finite family $\mathcal{B}\subset \mathcal{F}$ and  $m>n>\max \bigcup\mathcal{B}$, where $m$ is big enough there is $\Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,m]} - x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}\Vert_{\mathcal{B}}=0$ and 
\[\Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,m]} - x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[1,n]}\Vert_{\mathcal{F}}
= \Vert x\cdot\mathbbm{1}_{[n+1,m]}\Vert_{\mathcal{F}} \geq c.\]
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
The Proposition \ref{prop:fin:exh:equinormed} cannot be reversed, i.e. it may happen that in case when $\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})=\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})$ there may exist equinormed and non-compact sets. Let us consider $\mathcal{F} = \{\{1\}\} \cup \{ A\subset [2,+\infty) : |A|<\infty \}$. Then
\[
\Vert x\Vert_\mathcal{F} = \max\{|x_1|, \sum_{n=2}^{+\infty} |x_n|\}.
\]
Obviously $\mathrm{EXH}(\mathcal{F})=\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ and the set $A$ consisting of all points $x_n$, $n\geq 2$ given by
\[
x_{n,k} = \begin{cases} 1 & k\in\{1,n\} \\ 0 & {\text{otherwise}}
\end{cases}
\]
is equinormed, while $A-A$ is not equinormed.
head: environment

label: dirtheorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{dirtheorem}
If $\mathcal{F}$ is directed (that is, $\forall D, B \in \mathcal{F} \; \exists C \in \mathcal{F}: \; D \cup B \subseteq C$), then the equinormedness of $A \subseteq X_\mathcal{F}$ implies the equinormedness of $A-A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$A$ being equinormed means that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a finite subfamily $\mathcal{B} \subset \mathcal{F}$ such that $\forall x \in A: \; ||x||_\mathcal{F}-||x||_\mathcal{B}<\varepsilon$. It is possible (similarly as we did in Proposition \ref{prop:fin:exh:equinormed}) to find another finite subfamily $\mathcal{B}' \subset \mathcal{F}$ such that $$(\tau \subseteq \bigcup_\mathcal{B} \land \, \exists T \in \mathcal{F}: \; \tau \subseteq T) \implies \exists T' \in \mathcal{B}': \; \tau \subseteq T'.$$ In simple words, the sum over $\mathcal{B}$ is a finite subset of $\mathbb{N}$, collecting indices that are relevant in any manner for calculating the seminorm. We can choose all sets of these indices that exist as subsets in some set from $\mathcal{F}$, and put one representative for every such set in $\mathcal{B}'$ -- this subfamily is finite.
\newline
\newline
Let us take under consideration any $z \in A-A$. Since the norm $||z||_\mathcal{F}$ is defined as a supremum, without doubt there exists a set $R \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $||z||_\mathcal{F} - \sum_{n \in R} |z_n| < \varepsilon$. Our goal is to prove that $\mathcal{B}'$ is an appropriate seminorm for $A-A$, so for this purpose we can write $R$ as a sum of two separate sets $W \cup S$, where $W=R \cap \bigcup_\mathcal{B}$ and $S=R \setminus \bigcup_\mathcal{B}$. What we need is to bound $\sum_{n \in S} |z_n|$ with respect to $\varepsilon$.
For this purpose, naturally, we can exploit the fact that $z=x-y$ for some $x, y \in A$, and also $\sum_{n \in S} |z_n| \le \sum_{n \in S} |x_n| + \sum_{n \in S} |y_n|$. Therefore it is sufficient to bound one of these sums (and without loss of generality, both) with respect
to $\varepsilon$.
\newline
\newline
Let $P \in \mathcal{B}$ be the set which realises the supremum for $||x||_\mathcal{B}$. By assumption that $\mathcal{F}$ is directed, there exists $Q \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $P \cup R \subseteq Q$, so in particular $P\cup S\subseteq Q$. Hence, $$||x||_\mathcal{B}+\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| = \sum_{n \in P} |x_n|+\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le \sum_{n \in Q} |x_n| \le ||x||_\mathcal{F} \le ||x||_\mathcal{B}+\varepsilon,$$  so that indeed $\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le \varepsilon$. Finally, $$||z||_{\mathcal{B}'} \ge \sum_{n \in W} |z_n| \ge \sum_{n \in R} |z_n|-2\varepsilon > ||z||_\mathcal{F}-3\varepsilon.$$ Given that, for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a finite subfamily $\mathcal{B}' \subset \mathcal{F}$ such that $\forall z \in A-A: \; ||x||_\mathcal{F}-||x||_{\mathcal{B}'}<3\varepsilon$, $A-A$ is equinormed. This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The directedness of the family $\mathcal{F}$ is actually the very strong assumption. The only directed and hereditary family is the one given by all finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$: all directed families $\mathcal{F}$ have the same hereditary closure equal to $\mathcal{F}_{<\infty}$, hence for each such family the induced norm is equal to the norm of $\ell^1$. Still we decided to present this fact as it is a natural starting point for further investigations.
head: environment

label: def:cov:by:weight
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:cov:by:weight}
For any $0 \le \alpha \le 1$ and any family $\mathcal{E}(C)$ of nonempty subsets of a set $C$, we will say that a family $\mathcal{E}(C)$ belongs to $W_\alpha(C)$ (or \emph{covers at least $\alpha$ of $C$ by weight}) when, for any real sequence $x$ indexed over $C$, $$\exists C' \in \mathcal{E}(C) \; \sum_{i \in C'} |x_i| \ge \alpha\sum_{i \in C} |x_i|.$$
head: environment
name: Covering by weight

title: Remark
body_md:
Please note that this notion is, in a way, monotone with respect to $\alpha\in[0,1]$:
\[
\alpha'\leq\alpha \implies W_\alpha(C)\subseteq W_{\alpha'}(C).
\]
We may also easily observe that if $\mathcal{E}(C)\in W_1(C)$, then $C\in\mathcal{E}(C)$ and any nonempty family $\mathcal{E}(C)$ belongs to $W_0(C)$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Assume $C\subset\mathbb{N}$ satisfies $\#C=N$ and 
\[
\mathcal{E}(C) = \{ B\subset C : \#B = N-1 \}.
\]
Then $\mathcal{E}(C)$ covers at least $\alpha = 1 - \frac{1}{N}$ of $C$ by weight.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: For a family $\mathcal{F}$ of finite sets in $\mathbb{N}$ and any $N \in \mathbb{N}$, let us denote the family of all nonempty sets of the form $$B_N=B \cap [N+1,+\infty): B \in \mathcal{F}$$ as $\mathcal{F}_N$. $\mathcal{F}$ will be said to belong to the \emph{$(\lambda, \gamma)$-class of directedness} when $$\forall D \in \mathcal{F} \; \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \; \forall B \in \mathcal{F}_N:$$$$\exists \mathcal{E}(D) \in W_{1-\lambda}(D), \mathcal{E}(B) \in W_\gamma(B) \; \forall D' \in \mathcal{E}(D), B' \in \mathcal{E}(B) \; \exists C \in \mathcal{F}:$$$$D' \cup B' \subseteq C.$$
head: environment
name: Classes of directedness

title: Theorem
body_md: If $\mathcal{F}$ belongs to the $(0,c)$-class of directedness for some $c>0$, then the equinormedness of $A \subseteq \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ implies the equinormedness of $A-A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $A\subseteq\mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ is equinormed (as usual with respect to the family of seminorms given by the finite subsets of $\mathcal{F}$).
For any $F \in \mathcal{F}$ we can choose such $N \in\mathbb{N}$ that for any $B \in \mathcal{F}_N$ there exists $C \in \mathcal{F}$ ($F \subset C$) containing at least $c$ of $B$ by weight. Repeating the proof of Theorem \ref{dirtheorem}, we have a finite subfamily $\mathcal{B} \subset \mathcal{F}$ such that $\forall x \in A: \; ||x||_\mathcal{F}-||x||_\mathcal{B}<\varepsilon$. We can adopt as the new $N$ the largest of values of $N$ for $F \in \mathcal{B}$. We change the way $R$ is split into two sets so that $W=R \cap [1,N]$ and $S=R \cap [N+1,+\infty)$, intending to show that the sum $\sum_{n \in S} |x_n|$ can be bounded with respect to some function of $\varepsilon$.
\newline
\newline
Like previously, let $P \in \mathcal{B}$ be the set which realises the supremum for $||x||_\mathcal{B}$. By assumption that $\mathcal{F}$ belongs to the $(0,c)$-class of directedness, there exists $Q \in \mathcal{F}$ and $S' \subset S$ such that $P \cup S' \subseteq Q$ and $\sum_{i \in S'} |x_i| \ge c\sum_{i \in S} |x_i|$. Hence, $$||x||_\mathcal{B}+c\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le \sum_{n \in P} |x_n|+\sum_{n \in S'} |x_n| \le \sum_{n \in Q} |x_n| \le ||x||_\mathcal{F} \le ||x||_\mathcal{B}+\varepsilon,$$ so that indeed $\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le \frac{\varepsilon}{c}$. Defining the finite subfamily $\mathcal{B}' \subset \mathcal{F}$ on the basis of $[1,N]$ rather than $\bigcup_\mathcal{B}$, we complete the proof.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: If $\mathcal{F}$ belongs to the classes of directedness  $(\lambda, c')$ arbitrarily close to  $(0,c)$ (that is, there exists a sequence of such classes to which $\mathcal{F}$ belongs and its limit is by coordinates $(0,c)$), then the equinormedness of $A \subseteq \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ implies the equinormedness of $A-A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let us fix $\lambda\in(0,1)$ and $\delta\in(0,c)$ such that $\mathcal{F}$ belongs to $(\lambda,c-\delta)$ class of directedness. Then for any $F \in \mathcal{F}$ we can choose such $N \in\mathbb{N}$ that for any $B \in \mathcal{F}_N$ there exists $C \in \mathcal{F}$ containing at least $1-\lambda$ of $F$ and at least $c-\delta$ of $B$ by weight. Proceeding to the crucial inequality same as above, we arrive at $$(1-\lambda)||x||_\mathcal{B}+(c-\delta)\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le ||x||_\mathcal{B}+\varepsilon,$$ that is $\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le \frac{\lambda||x||_\mathcal{B}+\varepsilon}{c-\delta}$. Thus, choosing sufficiently small values of $\lambda$ and $\delta$, we can uniformly restrict the sum over $S$ dependent on $\varepsilon$ -- say, $\sum_{n \in S} |x_n| \le \frac{2\varepsilon}{c}$ -- what was to be proven.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: If $\mathcal{F}$ does not belong to the $(\lambda, 0)$-class of directedness for some $\lambda>0$, then the equinormedness of $A \subseteq \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ does not imply the equinormedness of $A-A$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: In this situation, there exists a set $F \in \mathcal{F}$ such that for any $N \in\mathbb{N}$ we can find nonempty $B \in \mathcal{F}_N$ with the property that any  $C \in \mathcal{F}$ ($B \cup C \neq \emptyset$) does not contain $1-c$ of $F$ by weight. Therefore,  we can assign values to elements of a sequence $x$ in such a manner that $\sum_{i \in F} |x_i|=1$, $\sum_{i \in B} |x_i|=c$ and $||x||_\mathcal{F}=1$. Composing the set $A$ from such sequences with increasingly distant sets $B$, we assure that $A$ is equinormed but $A-A$ is not.
head: environment

title: Open question
body_md: what can be said about the relation between the equinormedness of $A \subseteq \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{F})$ and the equinormedness of $A-A$ when $\mathcal{F}$ belongs to the classes of directedness arbitrarily close to $(0, 0)$?
head: manual

title: Example
body_md: We will denote the interval $[10^{i-1}+1, 10^i]$ as $D_i$; as an exception, let $D_1=[1,10]$. Let $\mathcal{D}ec$ be a family of finite sets in $\mathbb{N}$ which for some $i$ include as a subset the whole interval $D_i$ (called its \emph{principal interval}) and, for finitely many values of $j \ge 2i$, $\frac{1}{9}$ of the interval $D_j$ (in other words, $10^{j-1}$ elements from between $10^{j-1}+1$ and $10^j$). Clearly, $\mathcal{D}ec$ is not directed, as a sum of two sets from it can easily contain two whole intervals, which is never possible for a single set. However, for any given $D \in \mathcal{D}ec$ with a principal interval $D_i$, we can find such natural $k$ that $k \ge 2i$ and also $D_k$ lies further than any of the intervals featured in $D$; let $N=10^k+1$. Now, for any $B \in \mathcal{D}ec_N$, there exists some $C \in \mathcal{D}ec$ such that $D \subset C$, $C$ shares with $B$ all its secondary intervals, and $C$ contains any chosen $\frac{1}{9}$ of $B$'s principal interval. From here it follows that $C$ contains at least $\frac{1}{9}$ of $B$ by weight, and hence $\mathcal{D}ec$ belongs to the $(0, \frac{1}{9})$-class of directedness. The equinormedness of $A \subseteq \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{D}ec)$ implies the equinormedness of $A-A$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md: Let $\mathcal{D}ed$ be a family of finite sets in $\mathbb{N}$ which for some $i$ include as a subset the whole interval $D_{i_0}$ (called its \emph{principal interval}) and, for finitely many values of $i_{k+1} \ge 2i_k$, $\frac{1}{9}$ of the interval $D_{i_{k+1}}$ (in other words, $10^{i_{k+1}-1}$ elements from between $10^{i_{k+1}-1}+1$ and $10^{i_{k+1}}$). $\mathcal{D}ed$ is not directed for the exact same reason as $\mathcal{D}ec$. However, for any given $D \in \mathcal{D}ed$ with a principal interval $D_{i_0}$ and secondary intervals numbered to $D_{i_m}$, we can pick $N=10^{2i_m}+1$. Now, just like in case of $\mathcal{D}ec$, for any $B \in \mathcal{D}ed_N$, there exists some $C \in \mathcal{D}ed$ such that $D \subset C$, $C$ shares with $B$ all its secondary intervals, and $C$ contains any chosen $\frac{1}{9}$ of $B$'s principal interval. From here it follows that $C$ contains at least $\frac{1}{9}$ of $B$ by weight, and hence $\mathcal{D}ed$ belongs to the $(0, \frac{1}{9})$-class of directedness. The equinormedness of $A \subseteq \mathrm{FIN}(\mathcal{D}ed)$ implies the equinormedness of $A-A$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: An (undirected) \emph{hypergraph} is a pair $(V, E)$ where $V$ is a set whose elements are called \emph{vertices} and $E$ is a set of subsets of $V$ whose elements are called \emph{hyperedges}. Therefore, it is a generalization of a graph in which an edge is permitted to connect any number of vertices.
head: environment
name: Hypergraph

title: Definition
body_md: An incidence matrix uniquely representing a hypergraph with vertices $v_1, ..., v_n$ and hyperedges $e_1, ..., e_m$ is a $n \times m$ matrix with ones at the cell $(i, j)$ if $v_i$ is connected by the edge $e_j$ and zeros otherwise.
head: environment
name: Incidence matrix

title: Definition
body_md: The dual of a hypergraph represented by an incidence matrix $H$ is the hypergraph represented by the incidence matrix $H^T$.
head: environment
name: Dual of a hypergraph

title: Remark
body_md: Any hypergraph can be equivalently described as a bipartite graph with the vertices on one side representing the original vertices, the vertices on the other side representing the hyperedges, and the edges denoting which vertices are connected by a given hyperedge. The dual of any given hypergraph is described by its same bipartite graph with the roles of its sides reversed.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{matching} in a hypergraph is a set of hyperedges such that no two of them have a vertex they would both contain (they are all disjoint).
head: environment
name: Matching

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{vertex cover} in a hypergraph is a set of vertices such that every hyperedge contains at least one of them.
head: environment
name: Vertex cover

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{set cover} in a family of subsets of a given set is a collection of these subsets such that their union is the whole set. Equivalently, a set cover in a hypergraph is a set of hyperedges such that every vertex is contained in at least one of them.
head: environment
name: Set cover

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{fractional matching} in a hypergraph represented by an incidence matrix $H_{n,m}$ is a set of weights $w_1, ..., w_m$ such that $$\forall k \in \{1,...,n\} \; \sum_{i=1}^m H_{k,i}w_i \le 1.$$
head: environment
name: Fractional matching

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{fractional vertex cover} in a hypergraph represented by an incidence matrix $H_{n,m}$ is a set of weights $w_1, ..., w_n$ such that $$\forall k \in \{1,...,m\} \; \sum_{i=1}^n H_{i,k}w_i \ge 1.$$
head: environment
name: Fractional vertex cover

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{fractional set cover} in a hypergraph represented by an incidence matrix $H_{n,m}$ is a set of weights $w_1, ..., w_m$ such that $$\forall k \in \{1,...,n\} \; \sum_{i=1}^m H_{k,i}w_i \ge 1.$$
head: environment
name: Fractional set cover

label: th:furedi
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{th:furedi}
    The fractional matching number of any hypergraph is equal to its fractional vertex cover number.
head: environment
name: Füredi, 1981

title: Definition
body_md: An \emph{anticlique} in a hypergraph is a set of vertices such that no two of them have a hyperedge that would connect them (contain both of them).
head: environment
name: Anticlique

title: Definition
body_md: A \emph{fractional anticlique} in a hypergraph represented by an incidence matrix $H_{n,m}$ is a set of weights $w_1, ..., w_n$ such that $$\forall k \in \{1,...,m\} \; \sum_{i=1}^n H_{i,k}w_i \le 1.$$
head: environment
name: Fractional anticlique

title: Theorem
body_md: For any nonempty set $A$ and family of its nonempty subsets $\mathcal{E}(A)$, let us denote by $u(A, \mathcal{E}(A))$ the supremum on values of $\alpha$ such that $\mathcal{E}(A)$ covers at least $\alpha$ of $A$ by weight as given in Definition \ref{def:cov:by:weight}, and by $\mu^*(A, \mathcal{E}(A))$ the fractional anticlique number of the hypergraph created by mapping the elements of $A$ to vertices and the elements of $\mathcal{E}(A)$ to hyperedges. When, as we regularly assume, the union over the family $\mathcal{E}(A)$ covers the whole $A$ (and thus $u(A, \mathcal{E}(A))>0$), there occurs that $u(A, \mathcal{E}(A)) \cdot \mu^*(A, \mathcal{E}(A))=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The notion that that $\mathcal{E}(A)$ covers at least $\alpha$ of $A$ by weight means the following: allocating weights summing to $1$ to the elements of $A$ guarantees that at least one subset from $\mathcal{E}(A)$ has weight greater or equal to $\alpha$. By proportionality, it happens if and only if allocating weights summing to $\frac{1}{\alpha}$ to the elements of $A$ guarantees that at least one subset from $\mathcal{E}(A)$ will be weighed to at least~$1$. 

Therefore $\frac{1}{u(A, \mathcal{E}(A))}$ is the lower bound on the sums of weights having this last property. The fractional anticlique number $\mu^*(A, \mathcal{E}(A))$, on the other hand, is by definition the upper bound on the sums of weights where all subsets from $\mathcal{E}(A)$ are weighed to at most $1$. Yet let us take a number $\beta$ which is below one of these two bounds. Then there exists a configuration of weights assigned to the elements of $A$ and summing to $\beta$ such that each one of the subsets in the family $\mathcal{E}(A)$ is weighed at strictly less than $1$, which implies that $\beta$ is also below the other bound. This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The fractional anticlique number of any hypergraph is equal to its fractional set cover number.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: As we already know, the fractional set cover number of a hypergraph is equal to the fractional vertex cover number of its dual, the fractional anticlique number of a hypergraph is equal to the fractional matching number of its dual, and the equality of those two follows from Theorem \ref{th:furedi} (applied to that dual).
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: The Cover by Weight problem for a finite set $\mathcal{S}=\{s_1,...,s_N\}$ and a family $\mathcal{P}=\{P_1,...,P_M\}$ covering $\mathcal{S}$ is the problem of finding such value $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$ that for any sequence of nonnegative weights $(x_1,...,x_N)$ of elements of $\mathcal{S}$ such that $x_1+...+x_N=\alpha$ there exists at least one subset $P\in\mathcal{P}$ containing elements of total weight at least $1$, i.e. $\sum_{j\in P}x_j\geq 1$. We will denote the infimum of all such values of $\alpha$ by $\mu^*(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P})$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The Fractional Set Cover problem for a finite set $\mathcal{S}=\{s_1,...,s_N\}$ and a family $\mathcal{P}=\{P_1,...,P_M\}$ covering $\mathcal{S}$ is the
problem of finding such value $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$ that there exists a sequence of nonnegative weights $(y_1,...,y_M)$ of subsets $P\in\mathcal{P}$, such that for each element $s_i\in\mathcal{S}$ the sum of weights of sets $P$ containing $s_i$ is at least $1$. We will denote the infimum of all such values of $\beta$ by $\nu^*(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P})$.
head: environment

label: prop:lp:problems
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
\[
     \mu^*(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P})=\nu^*(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{P}).
     \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: As we can see $\tilde c=b$, $\tilde b = c$ and $\tilde A=A^T$. Hence the linear programming problem $\mu^*$ is dual to the linear programming problem $\nu^*$. This means that, by the strong duality theorem (cf. \cite[Section 6]{LinearProgramming}), there is $\max c^T x = \min\tilde c^T y$ what completes the proof.
head: environment
